summary: Slovenia's government says EU citizens need no visa or residence permit to enter and may do so with a valid identity card or passport. faq.question: Do I need a visa for Slovenia?
faq.answer: Slovenia's government says EU citizens need no visa and may enter with a valid identity card or passport. Nationals of the countries listed in Annex II of Regulation (EU) 2018/1806 are exempt from the visa requirement for stays of no more than 90 days in any 180-day period, and nationals of the countries listed in Annex I must hold a visa when crossing the external borders. The UK government says British travellers can visit the Schengen area, which includes Slovenia, visa-free on those terms.

faq.question: Is Slovenia in the Schengen Area?
faq.answer: Yes. The EU lists Slovenia among the Schengen area countries. The UK government tells people travelling on a full British citizen passport that visits to Schengen countries in the 180 days before they travel count towards the 90-day visa-free limit. Canada's travel advice says member states may temporarily reintroduce controls at internal borders, so you may have to pass through immigration controls when entering Slovenia even from another Schengen country.

faq.question: Will I need ETIAS for Slovenia?
faq.answer: ETIAS is currently not in operation and no applications are being collected; the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. The EU says applying costs EUR 20, though some travellers are exempt from the fee, and that an authorisation is valid for up to three years or until the passport expires, whichever comes first, for visa-exempt nationals travelling to any of 30 European countries.

faq.question: What currency does Slovenia use?
faq.answer: Canada's travel advice says the currency of Slovenia is the euro, that ATMs are rare in mountain regions or small villages, and to carry sufficient cash. No official source we could read describes how widely cards are accepted.

faq.question: Can I day-trip from Slovenia to Croatia or Italy?
faq.answer: The EU's Your Europe portal lists Italy, Croatia and Slovenia all in the Schengen area, and says you must show a valid passport or ID card when a country applies temporary border controls. The UK government says visits to other Schengen countries count towards the same 90-day visa-free limit.

levies.name: Tourist tax and promotional tax (turistična in promocijska taksa)
levies.exemptions: Exempt from the tourist tax, and so from the promotional tax: children up to 7; persons with a medical referral in natural spas; persons who show a disability decision or certificate; pupils and students on non-profit school excursions, and their leaders; people up to 18 at holiday camps of public-interest associations, and their leaders; volunteers dealing with the effects of natural disasters; Slovenian police on duty; temporary workers staying in the same accommodation for more than 30 days without a break; foreign nationals exempt under international treaties. Half the tourist tax is paid by people aged 7 to 18 and by people aged 18 to 30 staying in IYHF youth hostels. A municipality may add further exemptions.
levies.text: Slovenian citizens and foreigners staying overnight in accommodation pay the tourist tax and the promotional tax together with the payment for the overnight stay. The municipality sets the tourist tax at up to 2.5 euros, taking account of the type and category of accommodation, the season and the free services offered to tourists. The promotional tax is charged on top at 25 per cent of the tourist tax. Children up to 7 are exempt; people aged 7 to 18 pay 50 per cent.
